name: Kon Keu
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Glottolog: retired bookkeeping languoid (Sidwell 2015: same language as Hu [huo]); no Kon Keu-specific description

new_statements.quote: Minor syllables. As in other Northern Mon-Khmer languages, most non-compound words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, i.e. consisting of a major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable (cf. Shorto 1960). Minor syllables have a syllabic sonorant (such as m in θmphúp 'lung') or a (probably) non-contrasting vowel which I have written as a (kaʔà 'two'). [...] [p. 71:] There are two tones in Hu, namely, high (denoted by ´ over the vowel) and low (`).
new_statements.citation: Svantesson, Jan-Olof. 1991. "Hu - a language with unorthodox tonogenesis." In Jeremy H.C.S. Davidson (ed.), Austroasiatic Languages: Essays in honour of H. L. Shorto, 67-80. London: School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London.
new_statements.locator: p. 69, section 'Minor syllables' (tones: pp. 71-74, section 'Tones and vowels' and 'Vowel length or tones?')
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement

Printed p. 71 'Tones and vowels': 'There are two tones in Hu, namely…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hu (= Kon Keu) words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables; in a sesquisyllable the initial minor syllable (syllabic nasal or reduced vowel a) is unstressed and the final major syllable carries the stress and the tone, i.e. word prominence is fixed on the final (major) syllable; the language additionally has a two-way lexical tone contrast (high vs low) on the major syllable, derived from earlier vowel length.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; compounds are excluded from the generalisation ('most non-compound words'). Svantesson notes his material (a small vocabulary from one speaker, 1984) is too small for a complete synchronic analysis.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (phonological word shape: minor + major syllable); data are isolated citation forms elicited from one native speaker of Hu /xúʔ/ in Xiao Mengyang, Jinghong county, Sipsong Panna. Stress is mentioned only as a property of the sesquisyllabic template, not analysed as a separate system; tone is the contrastive suprasegmental.
new_statements.identity_note: konk1268 'Kon Keu' [kkn] is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid: a spurious/duplicate Ethnologue entry for Hu [huo] (Glottolog huuu1240; Chinese 户语 Huyu / 昆格语 Kunge; autonym xúʔ; exonym xɔn55 kɤt35 > 'Kon Keu'), per Sidwell 2015:9 and Hsiu 2015. The quoted source (Svantesson 1991) describes Hu of Xiao Mengyang, Jinghong county, Xishuangbanna, i.e. exactly the variety behind both codes. Any catalog entry should be filed under huuu1240 (Hu), with konk1268 noted as its retired duplicate.

sources.note: p. 69 'Minor syllables': most non-compound words are monosyllabic or sesquisyllabic, i.e. a major syllable preceded by an unstressed minor syllable; minor syllables have a syllabic sonorant or a non-contrasting vowel written a. pp. 71-74: Hu has two tones (high, low), reflexes of Proto-Palaungic vowel length; F0 and duration measurements given. No further statement on stress beyond the minor/major (iambic) word shape.
